chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said:

I asked him about two groups, one of which is the insurgents (baaghah) and the other is the just party (ahl al-adl), and the just party defeated the insurgents. He said: 'It is not permissible for the just party to pursue a fleeing enemy, nor to kill a captive, nor to finish off a wounded one. This is if no one remains from the insurgents and they do not have a force to which they can return. But if they have a force to which they can return, then their captive is killed, their fleeing one is pursued, and their wounded one is finished off.'

key_terms.بَاغِيَةٌ: Insurgents or rebels who deviate from the just ruler but are still Muslim
key_terms.عَادِلَةٌ: The just party, typically the army or government forces
key_terms.فِئَةٌ: A group or force, implying organized military capability
key_terms.يُجَازُ عَلَيْهِ: To finish off or kill the wounded

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for pursuing and killing rebels in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the jurisprudential distinction in *ahkam al-bagh* (rules of rebellion) based on the rebels' organizational status. It establishes that if the rebellious group is fragmented with no cohesive force to regroup, the victorious just party must exercise restraint by not pursuing the fleeing, killing captives, or finishing the wounded; however, if they possess an organized force, standard rules of war apply, allowing for pursuit, captivity, and finishing the wounded.
